strengths: Practical simplicity with minimal code changes (single line) and negligible computational overhead (0.4%), enabling broad adoption

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: 5 model sizes (66M-2B), 2 architectures (dense and MoE), 2 datasets, 2 LR schedules, with statistical validation via multiple random seeds and robustness checks
Consistent improvements across all tested configurations (1-3% terminal loss reduction), particularly strong on MoE models and warmup-stable-decay schedules
Demonstrated orthogonality to other optimizers (Muon, Blockwise LR), suggesting complementary benefits with cumulative gains

Insightful empirical findings on noise-dependent behavior of optimal p with good alignment between theory (Example 5.1) and practice (p=1.2), plus novel observation of improved training stability for MoE models
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: sign-power transformations exist in prior Powerball work (Yuan et al., 2019); the distinction of studying both p<1 and p>1 regimes is incremental

Severe theory-practice gap: convergence analysis only covers Adagrad, not Adam where experiments are conducted; theoretical claims about 'amplifying flat directions' lack formal justification; whether LLM training is truly 'noise-dominated' remains empirically unverified

Incomplete hyperparameter guidance: while claiming p=1.2 is 'highly robust,' it was tuned on a single small-scale experiment; Figure 6 reveals non-trivial batch-size dependence but no principled selection strategy is provided for new domains

Limited experimental scope: maximum model size is 2B (10B+ needed for modern standards), sparse comparison with recent optimizers (missing Sophia, Apollo, AdamMini), and modest downstream task improvements (mixed results, ≤1% gains)

Loose theoretical-empirical connection: the 1D uniform-distribution toy example abstracts away high-dimensional complexities; claimed benefits for MoE models have limited theoretical justification and only one MoE architecture tested

Modest effect sizes with incomplete statistical reporting: main results (Figures 3-4) appear to be single runs without error bars despite showing stochasticity, and downstream task gains are inconsistent across benchmarks

strengths: Exceptional practical simplicity with only one-line code change and negligible 0.4% wall-clock overhead enabling easy adoption

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse architectures (LLaMA, Qwen2MoE), scales (66M-2B parameters), datasets (C4, OpenWebText), and learning rate schedules with multiple random seeds reported
Generality demonstrated through successful integration with multiple optimizers (AdamW, Muon, Blockwise LR) showing complementary benefits
Insightful illustrative case study (Example 5.1) with both numerical and theoretical analysis revealing noise-to-signal dependence of optimal power parameter p
Thorough experimental methodology with detailed hyperparameter reporting and reproducibility information (Appendix B)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is applying the existing Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019) to modern LLM optimizers; Baiesi (2019) already combined power transformations with Adam; novelty is primarily in scaling rather than conceptual innovation

Modest empirical improvements: 15-26% FLOP reduction corresponds to ~2-3% wall-clock speedup for dense models; terminal loss improvements often <0.05 points (e.g., 3.09→3.07); gains appear constant rather than proportional in scaling laws

Incomplete understanding of mechanisms: claimed amplification of flat directions (abstract, Section 3) is never rigorously proven; speculative arguments about noise-dominated regimes lack formal verification for LLM training; unresolved questions about why MoE and wsd schedules benefit more are left for future work

Theoretical-practice mismatch: Section 5.2 analyzes AdagradPower rather than the Adam-based optimizer used; Theorems 5.8/5.11 prove only constant-factor acceleration, not convergence rate improvements; assumptions lack clear relevance to LLM training

Contradictory hyperparameter treatment: Section 4.6 clearly demonstrates optimal p depends on batch size (decreasing from 1.2 to 0.9 as batch size increases 512→8192), yet p=1.2 is used uniformly across all experiments; paper explicitly notes 'an even better p exists for MoE-specific training' but does not find it; lacks guidance for practitioners to select p in new settings

Statistical concerns: primary results (Figures 3, 4) show single runs without uncertainty quantification; only appendix provides multiple seeds; some differences appear within noise margins; missing comparisons with other recent optimizer improvements (curvature-based, variance reduction methods)

Insufficient treatment of prior work: key relationships to Powerball and Powerpropagation relegated to appendix despite significantly affecting novelty assessment; limited discussion of recent optimizer advances mentioned in Section 2

Limited scope of generalization claims: vision task validation only on ResNet-34 with CIFAR-10; downstream task improvements modest (0.5 points average on 6 benchmarks); claims of generalization beyond LLMs lack strong evidence

strengths: Practical utility: Single-line code change with minimal 0.4% wall-clock overhead makes the method genuinely deployable in production LLM training pipelines

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across diverse settings (2 architectures, 66M-2B parameters, 2 datasets, 2 LR schedules) with multiple random seeds, ablation studies, and scaling law analysis demonstrating consistency
Consistent improvements across diverse settings: Terminal loss improvements hold uniformly (0.015-0.028 points), with particularly strong gains on modern MoE models with warmup-stable-decay schedules

Novel batch size sensitivity analysis: Section 4.6's finding that optimal p decreases with batch size (p>1 in low-noise/small-batch, p<1 in high-noise/large-batch regime) is original and empirically validated

Theoretical insights in both regimes: Propositions 5.2-5.3 provide clear closed-form analysis with intuitive explanations; convergence guarantees for AdagradPower with meaningful acceleration constants
Orthogonality to modern optimizers: Successfully integrates with Muon and Blockwise LR with apparently additive gains, demonstrating broad applicability
Rigorous experimental methodology: Proper hyperparameter tuning, statistical validation across random seeds, multiple baseline comparisons, and honest treatment of limitations
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Convergence analysis applies to Adagrad not Adam; theoretical assumptions (5.6, 5.9) are not validated on real LLM gradient distributions; theory predicts p* via noise-to-signal ratio but doesn't directly explain why p=1.2 emerges empirically

Modest improvements at scale: Terminal loss improvements are 1-1.5% at 2B parameters; unclear if this translates to meaningful downstream benefits given limited downstream task evaluation (Table 1: only 6 tasks with small margins)

Incomplete explanations for key phenomena: MoE advantage is hypothesized but not rigorously analyzed; wsd scheduler benefits are noted but not deeply investigated; unclear why these settings particularly suit GradPower

Limited fundamental novelty: Core methodology (sign-power transformation) exists in prior Powerball work; contribution is primarily applying to modern LLM optimizers and studying p>1, which is incremental

Batch size dependence incompletely characterized: Figure 6-right shows significant p sensitivity (0.8-1.2 range); only studied on single architecture and two domains; no guidance for practitioners setting p a priori

Scaling validation limited to 2B parameters: All experiments ≤2B; unclear if improvements persist at 7B+ scales used in modern LLM training; scaling curves remain parallel but absolute gains don't increase

Empirical validation of theoretical assumptions missing: Propositions 5.2-5.3 rely on gradient distributions satisfying specific relationships, but this is not verified on actual LLM training trajectories
